If I die soon after this is posted, it will explain why there are so many 5 star reviews for this film…. 3 hours and 9 minutes?! I’m amazed I made it to the end. There’s at least 2 hours of wasted resources in this sequel. Somehow I still felt suspense at odd moments along the way, probably because Al Pacino is such an incredibly convincing actor along with others. I barely recognised Robert de Niro but another great job for him as always. After a sequence that made no sense to me and I never understood how it related or had any significance… It proceeds to start so punchy, so much action and uproar. Who in their right mind thought that should be followed by an entire hour of unnecessary context and boredom SOLELY IN Italian!? It was like the film was being narrated by that relative that takes every possible tangent and never gets to the good part until everyone’s lost interest. I zoned back in when the wife kicks off. Fair to say, I knew it wasn’t going to end well for her but I was rooting for her to just shoot the fool. I did not expect Michael to get so lost towards the end and for it to end that way but that’s not actually a negative at all, it’s a far more interesting narrative. As an edited down 90min film: decent worthwhile sequel. As it is: waste of my life I’ll never get back.

I technically started watching this on November 1st, but then discovered that the movie was split across 2 DVDs, and I only had 1, so it was finished on 11/2. Man, who knew the Godfather was like the god damn Lord of the Rings??? I do think as far as sequels go, it does cover interesting ground, and it's not a bad movie. I feel like modern sequels would be hung up on 'we have to bring back Marlin Brando and play the big hits again', but the movie had a lot of restraint (only 1 'I'll make him an offer he can't refuse'), covered new ground, and was thoughtful about how the 2 storylines, one in the past and one in the present, connect and parallel each other. That said: I do miss Marlin Brando.....I don't think it would make any sense for him to return considering how the first movie ended. My friend said it didn't really feel like there was a performance that had a bit of goofy energy to it, save for the old family friend, and I think that touches on why I miss seeing Brando so much. Sometimes I'm able to watch old movies and really connect with it, ala Casablanca or The Good, the Bad and the Ugly. The Godfather movies so far have been interesting watches, especially thinking about how much dads and guys seem to be incredibly fond of the movies, but it just doesn't resonate with me the same way. I don't know if it's a guy culture thing?

Alright so... i hate to be that guy because I hate people who use this as a "critique" when in reality its just their way of excusing their terrible attention spans but here we go.... HOLY FUUUUUUCK! THE GODFATHER PART II IS SO SO SO FUCKING BORING!! FUCK!! I came in swinging with good intentions, finally after years of fear and doubt i watched the first movie and honestly loved it. Now you'd think, wow! Double the story and double the star power with De Niro taking on a younger Vito Corleone! Question: what could go wrong? Answer: everything that doesn't fucking involve Robert De Niro! Jesus christ, Francis Ford! This was a lay-up, easily!! Everything related to Al Pacino in this is so dull. I know these were his first real movies but how is the most charismatic man of the late 70s, 80s and 90s such a void and vacuum of any and all emotion, intention and character. How, goddammit?! I don't buy a single second of this half-cocked psuedo- machiavellian bobbins. There's no hook. The film just expects you, on the good will created from the first, to just ride or die for this shit despite the fact that from seemingly out of nowhere, Michael (Pacino) went from war hero to vengeful but righteous mob boss to a stone cold boring heartless selfish fool who kills his family from the inside out? Fuck all the way off. As I said, De Niro is great - but fuck it, De Niro is great even in Dirty Grandpa so that ain't saying much. John Cazale is fantastic, a talent taken too soon. As for its merrits, it is clear from the rip that everyone involved is so much more confident making movies, given the first of the trilogy was "the big break" for most involved. Wie LeSchroeck in seiner Review gefordert hat, habe ich für das echte „ Pate -Erlebnis“ keine 24 Stunden nach Teil 1 jetzt Teil 2 nachgeschoben - und zumindest für mich nun die Gewissheit, dass die Trilogie sich nicht zu den für mich persönlich ganz großen Trilogien ( Herr der Ringe , Jurassic Park , Indiana Jones, … ) gesellen wird. Die Pate -Trilogie (bei der es bei mir wahrscheinlich vorerst bei 2 von 3 gesehenen Beiträgen bleiben wird) hat natürlich einen riesigen Scale, tolle Bilder, tolle Schauspielleistungen, tolle Musik und ich verstehe den Reiz den das alles ausübt - und es ist ja auch nicht so, dass ich hier 1 Sterne-Wertungen vergebe, auch wenn es sich bei so hoch gerankten, eigentlich universell verehrten Filmen ein wenig so anfühlt. Aber ich komme zurück zu Der Pate I , zu Goodfellas , Casino , The Irishman (der sich an der Unterkante von 4 Sternen bei der nächsten Sichtung kritisch gegen Der Pate I behaupten muss) aber auch Es war einmal in Amerika: Dass diese Filme richtig toll gemacht sind, ist gar keine Frage. Ob sie mich auch wirklich abholen, aber schon. Bei jedem einzelnen dieser Filme würde ich unterschreiben, dass sie mir zu lang sind - und lange Filme sind jetzt für mich nicht zwingend ein Problem. Viel mehr fühlen sich speziell diese langen Filme und vielleicht auch dieses Genre (obwohl es an sich eigentlich spannend und reizvoll ist) für mich zu lang - oder auch „langatmig“ - an. Vielleicht liegt es - wie zuvor schonmal angemerkt - daran, dass ein so großer Zeitraum erzählt und komplexe Charakterentwicklungen vergegenwärtigt werden sollen. Und ich erkenne ein ähnliches Problem bei vielen Biopics, die ihre Stationen ein wenig „abarbeiten“, aber eben auch nicht bei allen. Dazu kommt bei Francis Ford Coppola , dass ich dieses Gefühl schon bei Dracula und leider auch Apocalypse Now (Redux) hatte - erfreulicherweise nicht bei The Conversation . Bei Martin Scorsese ist das etwas anderes, da hier gefühlt etwas mehr Sog drin ist und mit Shutter Island, The Wolf of Wallstreet und The Departed Filme mit ähnlicher Länge hervorragend funktionierten. Bei Sergio Leone s Western ging es mir ebenfalls anders, sodass ich denke, dass hier einiges an persönlicher Präferenz und Bindung zu, sowie Interesse an den Figuren den Ausschlag gibt. Unterm Strich finde ich es immer schade, wenn Werke, die bei anderen große Begeisterung bis zu Verehrung hervorrufen, bei mir etwas versanden - letztendlich sind nämlich diese Schätze am leichtesten zu finden und versprechen oft eine höhere Erfolgsquote. Hier wusste ich, mich bewusst nicht zu sehr hypen zu lassen. Und an sich ist die Trüffelsuche, das Kopfüberreinstürzen in unsere favorisierten Sub-Genres, die jahrelange Suche nach dem unentdeckten Diamant, der genau deinen Geschmack trifft, den du aber in Toplisten vergebens gesucht hast, doch auch eines der Dinge, die dieses Hobby so schön machen. Ich nehme mit, dass der Mafiafilm als Genre sich bei mir nicht ganz oben einreiht, habe - wenn man das so betrachten will - eine „Wissenslücke“ geschlossen und hoffe einfach, dass der nächste unbekannte Film wieder ein persönlich größerer Kracher wird. Und ja: Ich habe jetzt echt wenig zum Film an sich gesagt. Aber ich finde, dass manchmal das Zusammenbringen von Erwartungshaltung und Kontext genau so viel wert sein kann, wie eine weitere Abhandlung der Leistungen und ikonischen Szenen. Letzteres überlasse ich hier den wirklich begeisterten Zuschauenden - denn ich bin mir sicher, dass deren Schilderungen (dank mitschwingender Affektion) viel schöner zu lesen sind, als alles, was ich hier inhaltlich da lassen kann, ganz besonders da sich mein Eindruck in der „unspektakulären“ Mitte des Spektrums wiederfindet.

The pacing also feel slower, and constantly switching between Michael’s decline and Vito’s rise  makes the story feel less focused. The alternating stories of Vito and Michael do not always strengthen each other. Michael’s dealings with Roth and Pentangeli require close attention: he gives different people different accounts of the attempted assassination, testing their responses while concealing his own conclusions. Returning to Vito’s beginnings interrupts that process for a more episodic account of his advancement. Both stories contain excellent material, but their combination has stretches where the comparison between generations matters more than the developing drama. I find the film considerably more compelling in its individual confrontations than as a continuous experience. Vito’s scenes are seductive for understandable reasons. De Niro makes courtesy an active part of the character’s intelligence. He listens, accommodates, waits for people to reveal what they want. His dealings with the landlord who threatens to evict a widow are funny because everyone understands the threat without requiring him to deliver it. The landlord becomes extravagantly helpful; Vito can remain gracious. Here is a man discovering how much violence can accomplish after it has ceased to be visible. Calling these episodes merely nostalgic would miss their shrewdness. Nevertheless, the selection of Vito’s victims makes his rise unusually easy to accept. Fanucci is an extortionist who has already cost him his job; Don Ciccio murdered his family. We receive ample preparation for wanting both men dead. Michael’s violence, meanwhile, increasingly damages people whose vulnerability the film has established. The contrast is dramatically effective, but it also gives the father considerably more favourable circumstances in which to become a murderer. There is room to question how much of the apparent moral distance between these men comes from their characters, and how much comes from the stories Coppola chooses to tell about them. Gordon Willis’s photography adds another complication. The softer textures of the early New York material give Vito’s world the appeal of something recovered from old photographs. The past acquires a beauty that can survive our knowledge of what happened there. This is an expressive choice, and a fruitful one: the family’s origins can look precious while containing the habits that will destroy it. But the attraction is so strong that Michael’s present sometimes feels like a prolonged punishment for losing a world the film has been especially generous in constructing. The tension between exposure and affection remains unresolved. That is interesting, though it does not automatically make every return to the past necessary. The conversation between Tom Hagen and Pentangeli is more exact about the family’s morality. Their discussion of Roman conspirators turns suicide into an arrangement through which a disgraced man can secure his relatives’ future. Duvall’s professional composure matters enormously. Tom can offer reassurance while communicating something appalling, and the reassurance is part of what makes it appalling. Pentangeli understands him. The men do not need to abandon affection, manners or shared memories to conduct this transaction. Those things help them conduct it. John Cazale gives the film its most painful account of what being protected by this family can mean. Fredo wants Michael to acknowledge that being looked after has also meant being dismissed. His insistence that he is intelligent is embarrassing, angry and terribly exposed. Cazale allows those feelings to coexist; Fredo’s grievance does not become ridiculous simply because he expresses it badly. Michael’s replies keep returning to authority and useful information. He can investigate his brother’s betrayal much more readily than he can respond to the humiliation behind it. Pacino is equally formidable when Kay tells Michael about the abortion. Until then, his belief that he can manage her unhappiness remains intact. Her revelation confronts him with an action taken beyond his permission, inside the family he treats as his justification for everything. The sudden physical violence exposes how little space his assurances ever allowed her. Keaton has too few opportunities to exist outside Michael’s crisis, but here she changes the terms of the encounter. His power has been extensive throughout the film; for once, it is plainly insufficient. The final dinner flashback provides the most convincing use of the film’s structure. Fredo congratulates Michael on joining the Marines while the others object. Coming after Fredo’s murder, that small kindness restores something Michael’s judgment of his brother has excluded. The younger Michael’s separation from the family also changes the meaning of his eventual solitude: he once sat apart because he had chosen another life. This return to the past alters the present with extraordinary economy. It is the passage that most clearly demonstrates what the larger construction can achieve, and why its less productive interruptions remain frustrating.

Continua uma belezinha! 1. Trama Filme que faz parte da discussão onde a sequência é muito melhor que o filme original... O que fica claro aqui é que Coppola realiza algo tão sublime quanto ao filme anterior e é notável sua experiência em algumas situações. No fim das contas,essa franquia é prestigiada justamente por ter dois filmes no mesmo patamar. O diretor consegue manter a ótima cinematografia com muita coisa chamando atenção e o assuntos mafiosos ainda continuam impressionando. A história se eleva aqui por trabalhar bem o presente e o passado de uma forma balanceada,algo que faz o espectador entender todo o início de uma história e onde ela chegou. Com poucos personagens,diferente do primeiro,temos um filme que valoriza muito o tempo do protagonista e suas atitudes. As participações femininas também ganha muito mais espaço aqui do que no filme anterior e todas as atrizes conseguem se apresentar muito melhor que no filme anterior. 2. Direção Coppola trabalhava dia e noite nesse filme aqui,mesmo trabalhando também em "A Conversação" que também tinha sido lançado em 1974. Se comparar os dois filmes vimos uma diferença absurda de trabalhos. O diretor tira um pouco mais o peso em certas cenas em comparação ao primeiro. Temos muito mais diálogos aqui do que trocas de tiros e violência escancarada. E isso torna o filme mais maduro e inteligente justamente para casar perfeitamente com o momento atual do protagonista. 3. Al Pacino O ator continua no mesmo ritmo do primeiro,aumentou apenas o seu jeito frio de executar e escolher suas as coisas ao seu redor. O olhar frio sempre antecipa algum acontecimento trágico e todos os acontecimentos são fáceis de entender dada certas circunstâncias. E novamente tivemos o Oscar pregando peça escolhendo Art Carney vencedor na categoria Melhor Ator ao invés de premiar Al Pacino. 4. Robert de Niro Temos apenas o segundo grande filme do ator,anteriormente realizando uma participação convincente em "Caminhos Perigosos". Papel que foi o suficiente para chamar atenção de Coppola para chamá-lo para integrar o elenco desse aqui. A sua preparação para viver Vito Corleone foi uma barra,o diretor exigiu que o ator morasse cerca de quatro meses na região da Sicilia para aprender o idioma e a forma de viver do povo local. De Niro foi o vencedor do Oscar de Melhor Ator Coadjuvante por esse personagem. 5. Nota Coppola entrega mais uma obra-prima e assim como o primeiro temos aula de cinema que ficará marcada pra sempre na história do cinema. Tudo feito aqui e lá,moldou a forma de fazer filmes mafiosos.  E todas as insistências de Coppola e suas loucuras nos sets de filmagem resultaram em dois filmes que são apenas um no quesito clássico absoluto.
